Confit is a cooking process where food, most traditionally waterfowl legs, is salted and then cooked slowly at low temperatures submerged in fat, which historically served as a method of preservation. While deep frying uses high heat, confit is typically done around 90°C (200°F). The technique is a specialty of southwestern France and is central to dishes like cassoulet and rillettes. The term also applies to fruits preserved in sugar and to various slow-cooked condiments like onion or garlic confit.
